**Verdict:** Partly right. You read the labels well, but your pick needs more thought.

**What you got right:** You wrote the fibers and percentages clearly. You also thought about sweat, which is the right worry for Riyadh in July.

**What to fix:** Two things are off. First, you only gave two pieces. The task asked for three. Second, silky does not mean cool. Viscose and nylon can feel smooth, but nylon is a plastic fiber like polyester. Plastic fibers do not let air through well. Think of a rain jacket: it feels slick, but you sweat inside it. Smooth feel is not the same as airflow. Also, your first shirt has 30% polyester and 17% stretch fiber, so only 53% is cotton. That one will breathe less than pure cotton. Your second shirt may be the better pick, but the reason is not "silky."

**Try this:** Hold each shirt to your mouth and blow through it. Note which one lets more air through. Then add a third piece and pick again.

**Verdict:** Partly right. You spotted the chino twill, but the thobe is mixed up.

**What you got right:** The chinos with a diagonal line are twill. Good eye. You also saw that the shiny cloth has tight, straight lines, which fits satin.

**What to fix:** You called the thobe "twill," but "over and under" is plain weave. Plain weave is like a checkerboard: one up, one down, every time. Twill is a staircase, with lines that slant. Your thobe has no diagonal, so it is plain. Also, a tablecloth is not always satin. Satin threads float long over the top, like a skater gliding. Look for a smooth, glassy surface with no visible grid.

**Try this:** Hold your phone camera close to the thobe cloth. Zoom in and look for a grid of tiny squares. Then look at your chinos and find the diagonal.

feedback.18:
**Verdict:** Partly right. You got the idea that woven patterns are part of the cloth, but two details are off.

**What you got right:** You saw that the jacquard pattern is part of the shirt and not just sitting on top. That is the key sign of a woven-in pattern. You also noticed that embroidery is different from the rest of the cloth.

**What to fix:** First, jacquard is woven, not knitted. Woven cloth has threads crossing at right angles, like a basket. Knit cloth is made of loops, like a sweater. Check a cut edge or look closely: loops mean knit, a grid means woven. Second, the pattern is not sewn in. It is made on the loom when the cloth is made. Sewing happens later, when the cloth is made into a shirt. Third, embroidery raised on the inside is unclear. Embroidery is raised on the front. On the back, you should see stitches or loose thread ends. You also did not mention the print.

**Try this:** Pick up your printed item. Turn it over. Write one line: is the back plain or faded?

**What you got right:** You told me the truth about what you have. That is better than guessing. Many designers start with no blazer, so this is fine.

**What to fix:** The answer does not say what you found, so the lesson is not done yet. You probably thought the test needed your own jacket. It does not. Any jacket works.
